title: Marig-on Marathon 2026 Review: Northern Samar's Eagles-Club 42K at the Edge of the Pacific
seo_title: Marig-on Marathon 2026 Review | Catarman Northern Samar Philippines
meta_description: Marig-on Marathon 2026: September 20 in Catarman, Northern Samar. A grassroots full marathon from the Samarnon Eagles Club — one of the Philippines' most off-the-grid 42K races, reviewed in full.
dek: Set for 20 September 2026 in Catarman, Northern Samar, this Eagles Club-organised full marathon brings 42.195 kilometres to one of the Philippines' least-visited provinces — a Pacific-facing island of raw coastline, coconut country, and genuine community race spirit.
verdict: The Marig-on Marathon is a community-organised full marathon in Catarman, the capital of Northern Samar — a province that sits on the Pacific-facing edge of the Eastern Visayas, far from the standard Philippine racing circuit of Manila, Cebu, and Davao. Organised by the Marig-on Norte Samarnon Eagles Club, a civic organisation rather than a professional race-management company, this event carries an authentic grassroots character that is increasingly rare in an era of corporate-branded running festivals. The full marathon distance — all 42.195 kilometres — is the centrepiece, supported by a half marathon, 10K, and 5K, making this one of the very few marathons held anywhere in Samar. The trade-offs are substantial and honest: September is the peak of the Philippine typhoon season, and Northern Samar's Pacific exposure means it catches weather systems before anywhere else in the archipelago. Registration details, course maps, and aid-station plans have not been published, which is par for the course with a civic-club race but demands patience and flexibility from travelling runners. For the runner who has already done the Manila and Cebu marathons and wants a 42K story that nobody else in their running club has, the Marig-on Marathon delivers something genuinely singular — a full marathon in a province that most Filipinos have never visited, organised by people who are doing it for the love of their community rather than a profit margin. This is not a race for a personal best or a seamless race-cation. It is a race for the adventure of it.

sections.heading: Catarman and Northern Samar: Where the Typhoons Land First
paragraphs: Northern Samar is not a place most travellers — Filipino or foreign — put on their itinerary. It is the northernmost province of Samar Island, facing the Philippine Sea and the open Pacific, and its economy runs on copra, abaca, fishing, and the remittances of overseas workers rather than tourism [2]. Catarman, the provincial capital, is a town of roughly 100,000 people with a modest airport, a university, and the kind of unhurried provincial rhythm that feels a world away from Metro Manila — because it is: the flight from Manila takes about 90 minutes, and the ferry from Cebu crosses the Samar Sea overnight.

The province is known among Filipinos for its raw coastline — the pink-sand beach of Biri Island's rock formations, the Lalaguna mangrove forest, and the waves off Capul Island — but it is equally known for being first in the path of Pacific typhoons. The geography is dramatic and humbling: the San Bernardino Strait separates Northern Samar from Luzon, and when storm systems build over the Philippine Sea, Samar takes the initial impact before they track westward across the archipelago. This is not a footnote — it is the defining fact of life here, and it is the single most important thing to understand about running a marathon in Catarman in September.

The Marig-on Norte Samarnon Eagles Club is a chapter of the Fraternal Order of Eagles, a nationwide civic organisation that runs charitable and community-service programmes across the Philippines — scholarships, medical missions, feeding programmes [1]. That a local Eagles chapter would decide to stage a full marathon says something about the ambition and community pride behind this event: this is not a professional race organiser with a portfolio of events, but a group of civic volunteers who want to put their town on the map. The result is a race with real heart, even if the polish and predictability of a corporate race weekend are absent.

sections.heading: The Race: Four Distances Anchored by a Full 42K
paragraphs: The Marig-on Marathon offers four distances: the full 42.195 kilometres, a 21.1-kilometre half marathon, a 10K, and a 5K — a comprehensive spread that accommodates everyone from first-time fun runners to serious marathoners [1]. The full marathon is the headline act, and in a country where 42K races outside the major cities are genuinely scarce, the mere existence of a marathon in Catarman is noteworthy. Most Philippine marathons cluster in Metro Manila, Cebu, and Davao; a full marathon in Northern Samar is an outlier by any measure.

The venue is listed simply as Catarman, Northern Samar, without a specific start-line address — typical of a civic-club race where the town itself is the venue and the course will be marked through public roads with barangay-level permits rather than the closed-highway arrangements of a major-city event [1]. Runners should expect a course that mixes the poblacion (town centre) streets with provincial roads radiating into the surrounding countryside, likely passing through coconut plantations, rice paddies, and coastal barangays. The terrain in Northern Samar is gently rolling rather than mountainous, with the island's interior spine of hills rising further south; the immediate Catarman area is relatively flat by Samar standards.

Registration details have not been announced as of mid-2026, which means interested runners will need to monitor the Eagles Club's Facebook page or the Pinoy Fitness listing for updates [1]. This is not a race where you book six months in advance and receive a confirmation email with a QR code — it is a race where you send a message, wait for a reply, and show up with cash and a sense of humour. For runners accustomed to the frictionless online registration portals of major events, this will feel like stepping back in time. For runners who have done grassroots Philippine races before, it will feel familiar and, in its own way, endearing.

sections.heading: September in Samar: The Weather Factor
paragraphs: September is the peak of the Philippine typhoon season, and Northern Samar — facing the open Pacific — is statistically one of the most exposed locations in the entire archipelago [3]. Average daytime temperatures hover around 30-32°C with humidity rarely dropping below 80 percent, and September is one of the wettest months of the year across the Eastern Visayas, with monthly rainfall totals that can exceed 300 millimetres [3]. Tropical cyclones that form over the Philippine Sea typically track westward, and Samar Island is often the first landmass they encounter — which means race day could range from hot and humid with scattered thunderstorms to a full weather cancellation if a typhoon makes landfall.

The organisers, as a civic club rather than a professional race-management company, are unlikely to have the kind of contingency infrastructure — weather-monitoring teams, medical tents every two kilometres, real-time course-adjustment protocols — that major-city marathons deploy for heat and storm risk [1]. Runners need to come prepared to be substantially self-sufficient: carry your own hydration between whatever aid stations are provided, bring electrolytes and salt tablets, and have a plan for what to do if the weather turns severe. The local government and the Eagles Club will almost certainly cancel or postpone the race if a typhoon warning is in effect, but communication may be informal — a Facebook post rather than an email blast.

That said, September mornings in Samar can be beautiful: the light over the rice fields, the coconut palms still in the pre-storm humidity, the quiet of a provincial town before the heat builds. Runners who embrace the unpredictability and show up with flexible expectations will find the atmospheric conditions part of the adventure rather than a reason to stay home. Just do not plan on a personal best [3].

sections.heading: Getting There, Staying There, and the Samar Travel Reality
paragraphs: Catarman has a small domestic airport (IATA: CRM) served by Philippine Airlines from Manila, with flights taking about 90 minutes — but schedules are limited, and cancellations are common during the typhoon season [2]. The alternative is a longer overland-and-ferry journey: fly to Tacloban (Leyte) and take a bus or van north through the San Juanico Strait and across Samar Island, a trip of roughly five to six hours that passes through some of the most scenic rural landscapes in the Eastern Visayas. There is also a ferry from Cebu City to Calbayog (the neighbouring city in Samar province) that runs overnight. None of these options is quick or convenient by the standards of a Singapore or Bangkok marathon, and that is precisely the point — reaching Catarman is part of the experience.

Accommodation in Catarman is limited to a handful of small hotels, inns, and pension houses, none of them luxury by any standard. The Rhonson's Hotel and the Catarman Mandarin are the closest things to business-class lodging, and even they are modest — clean, air-conditioned, functional [2]. Book well ahead of race weekend, because the influx of runners and their families will fill the available rooms quickly in a town where the hospitality infrastructure is not built for surges. Local food is a highlight: Samar is known for its seafood (the crabs and prawns from the Samar Sea are genuinely excellent), and the town market is the place to eat if you want to carbo-load on pancit (stir-fried noodles) and fresh buko (young coconut) rather than pasta and sports gels.

Cash is essential — Catarman has ATMs, but they are unreliable, and many small establishments do not accept cards. Bring enough pesos to cover your race registration, accommodation, food, and transport, and do not assume you can withdraw more on arrival. Mobile data coverage exists in the town centre but can be patchy on the race route, so download any maps or race information before you leave your hotel [2].

sections.heading: Should You Run the Marig-on Marathon?
paragraphs: If you are a local runner in the Eastern Visayas — someone based in Tacloban, Calbayog, or anywhere on Samar or Leyte — the Marig-on Marathon is a genuinely rare opportunity to run a full 42K without flying to Manila or Cebu. The community atmosphere of a civic-club race, where the organisers are your neighbours rather than a distant corporation, is something that larger races cannot replicate, and the chance to run a full marathon on home ground in Samar is worth every logistical inconvenience [1].

If you are a domestic runner from elsewhere in the Philippines who has already ticked off the Manila, Cebu, and Davao marathons and is looking for a 42K adventure that will genuinely stand out in your race CV, the Marig-on Marathon is one of the most unusual entries on the Philippine calendar. Combine it with a few days of exploring Samar's wild coastline — Biri Island, the Sohoton Caves, the rock formations of Capul — and you have a trip that is as much about discovery as it is about running. But temper your expectations: this is a grassroots event with all the unpredictability that implies, and you should come prepared to be flexible about everything from the start time to the course markings [1].

If you are an international marathon tourist, be honest with yourself about what you are signing up for. The Marig-on Marathon is not the Angkor Wat Half Marathon or the Bali Marathon — there is no expo, no pace team, no closed-road guarantees, and no English-language customer-support line. Getting to Catarman requires domestic flights or long overland journeys, and the typhoon risk in September is real and non-trivial. If you want an off-the-grid marathon story that very few foreign runners can claim, this is it — but do not book non-refundable flights, and have a backup plan. For the right kind of runner, the kind who values a unique experience over a seamless one, the Marig-on Marathon offers something that no major-city marathon can: a full 42K in a place that almost no race reaches, run by people who are doing it for the love of their community [1].
